15.1.name: 15.01.md
15.1.text: Is a member function that is defined by the base class. Unlike ordinary member functions--which are inherited without change--a virtual function can, and is expected, to be overridden by the derived class. Designating a function as virtual allows us to distinguish between those operations that are common from those that are specific to inherited class'. An important characteristic of a virtual function is that its call, if done through a reference or a pointer, is dynamically bound. This means that "[d]epending on the type of the object to which the reference or pointer is bound, the version in the base class or in one of its derived classes will be executed." (p. 595) As such, a virtual functions is evaluated at runtime, as opposed to member functions that are evaluated at compile time.

15.2.name: 15.02.md
15.2.text: The private specifier restricts access to the class members. Only member functions of the same class or friends of the class is granted access to private members. This restriction applies to derived classes as well--a derived class cannot access the base class private members. The protected specifier allows derived classes to access the base class private members while still "protecting" them from public access. In short, protected maintains the concept of encapsulation in context of class inheritance.

15.8.name: 15.08.md
15.8.text: A static type is the type of a variable or an expression that is known at compile time. "It is the type with which a variable is declared or that an expression yields. The dynamic type is the type of the object in memory that the variable or expression represents." (p. 601) It is not known until runtime. Put differently, a static type is the type that a variable or an expression 'ought' to have, which is locked during compilation, and the dynamic type is the 'actual' type the variable holds or the expression yields at runtime. An expression that is neither a reference nor a pointer will always have identical static and dynamic types. A reference or a pointer, on the other hand, could have a different static type from its dynamic type at runtime.

15.24.name: 15.24.md
15.24.text:
Classes that are related by inheritance. The destructors of such classes are responsible for freeing the resources of their objects. The base class must define a virtual destructor, which may be overridden by the derived classes. This is important so that compiler knows which destructor to call when an object of these classes is destroyed.

This is especially important when dealing with objects of polymorphic types, objects whose static and dynamic types can differ, as in the case with classes related by inheritance. (p. 605) Designating the destructor as virtual tells the compiler to generate code that will resolve which destructor to run based on dynamic type of the object at runtime, as opposed to the static type at compile time, as what would happen if destructor were a non-virtual functions. This will ensure that the appropriate destructor is called with such types.

Furthermore, if a derived class allocates memory on the heap, it must override the base class virtual destructor to include the necessary steps to free the resources it has allocated for its members.

15.32.name: 15.32.md
15.32.text:
Query has a synthesized copy-control operations. When it is copied, moved, and assigned the appropriate synthesized operation will memberwise copy, move or assign its data members. Query has only one data member q, which is a shared_ptr. As smart pointer, q would adjusts its reference counter according to the effect of the copy-control operation on it.

When a Query object is destroyed, Query's destructor will run the shared_ptr q's destructor. If q's reference counter is 0, a virtual call to the destructor of Query_base will be made that will run the appropriate derived class' destructor based on the dynamic type q.

15.33.name: 15.33.md
15.33.text: Query_base is an abstract base class. It only provides a common interface to its derived classes. It cannot create objects of its own directly. As such, it cannot be copied, moved, assigned or destroyed.

15.37.name: 15.37.md
15.37.text:
1) The constructor AndQuery, OrQuery and NotQuery parameters' types must be

changed from Query to shared_ptr<Query_base>

2) The parameter(s) and the return type of the overloaded operators, with the

exception of <<, must be change from type Query to shared_ptr<Query_base>

3) All the calls to rep and eval must use the -> access member operator

instead of the "." Member access operator.

4) As a result of 3, the virtual function rep in Query_base must be public,

otherwise it will not be accessible through dereferencing the shared_ptr<Query_base> within the derived classes. Alternatively, we could have the derived classes befriend Query_base (but that is awkward syntax). Note: private or protected access specifier will not work, because dereferencing the shared_ptr involves derived-to-base conversion, which has its own subtle restriction on accessibility. (p 613-614

5) The same would apply to eval in Query_base.

6) Query class must define a conversion operator (with a public access

specifier) from Query to shared_ptr<Query_base>

7) Query's constructor that takes a shared_ptr (and the conversion operator)

must be public in order to be accessible to users. This is so for the same reason mention in 4.

For an implementation, see 15.37a.cpp.

15.40.name: 15.40.md
15.40.text:
If rhs member returned an empty set: Both right.begin() and right.begin() would return equal iterators, denoting a range of zero. Consequently, the lines->insert operation would have no effect.

If lhs member returned an empty set: ret_lines would be initialized to an empty set by make_shared, because both begin and end iterators would be equal, and therefore, the call to make_shared would be equivalent to

```cpp
auto ret_lines = std::make_shared<std::set<line_no>>();
```

Since a set can grow dynamically, the operation that follows (ret_lines->insert) would still be safe.

If both members returned an empty set: The above two behaviours will occur and we end up with an empty ret_lines. In other words, result of the OrQuery is that neither word (or a set or words) is found in the text.

Her Daddy says when the wind blows
